newsitem.title: USA: U.S. toxic fish warnings up in 1996.
newsitem.headline: U.S. toxic fish warnings up in 1996.

text.p: The number of U.S. lakes and rivers where fish were considered dangerous to eat jumped 26 percent in 1996 from 1995, the Environmental Protection Agency said Wednesday.
The rise in fish consumption warnings was largely due to improved monitoring and reporting rather than an increase in pollution, it said.
Water bodies under advisories made up 5 percent of the nation's river miles and 15 percent of total lake acreage, including all of the Great Lakes.
People had to watch out about eating fish from those rivers and lakes mainly because the waters were polluted with mercury, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), chlordane, dioxins and DDT, EPA said.

Warnings varied but were mainly for recreational and subsistence fishing. Some recommended no fish should be eaten, others said limited amounts could be eaten, or suggested only certain types of fish should be avoided. Some warnings were targeted at men, others at women and children.
"The populations with the highest potential of increased risk are those who routinely eat freshwater fish from a single location or region that is known to be impacted by contamination," EPA said.

Foetuses are the most sensitive to the five chemicals that most often trigger warnings. Other groups who face higher risk from toxic waters are native Americans and Asian Americans who eat a lot of fish, the agency said.
